Q8137.L1t: Act of State is one of several doctrines in public international law and domestic courts that limit how national courts deal with the conduct of foreign States.
Q8137.L2t: The doctrine is distinct from State immunity: it is a rule of judicial restraint about the validity of sovereign acts, not a rule about who may be sued.
Q8137.L3t: Under the doctrine, courts regard questions about the lawfulness of a State's sovereign conduct as sensitive matters of foreign relations that are for the political branch to decide, not for judges.
Q8137.L4t: The doctrine means that deciding whether a State has committed an alleged tort is a matter for the executive and not for the courts.
Q8137.L2f: The doctrine was first created by the International Court of Justice as a rule binding on States in their treaty relations.
Q8137.L3f: The doctrine rests on the premise that judges have the expertise and constitutional role to evaluate foreign State conduct, so that such questions are for the courts to resolve.
Q8137.L4f: The doctrine means that courts are well placed to assess whether a State has committed an alleged tort.
Q8137.cand_true: The act of State doctrine denotes that the assessment as to the existence of an alleged tort committed by a State belongs to the executive and not the courts
Q8137.cand_wrong1: The act of State doctrine denotes that the courts are well placed to assess the existence of an alleged tort committed by the State
Q8137.cand_wrong2: The act of State doctrine denotes that all State acts attract immunity

Q6120.L1t: Estimates of historical GDP per capita are built by combining national accounts and archival data, then converting to a common currency using PPP and constant prices.
Q6120.L2t: The 2011-price PPP series used by long-run databases such as the Maddison Project and Our World in Data puts most pre-industrial economies at a few hundred to a few thousand dollars per person.
Q6120.L3t: The US in 1850 was already a fairly rich agrarian economy that was beginning to industrialize, and its real income per person was roughly double the roughly $1,500 level of the early 1800s, which puts it in the low thousands rather than in the hundreds or the many thousands.
Q6120.L4t: In 1850 US GDP per capita in 2011 PPP dollars was about three thousand dollars.
Q6120.L2f: The Maddison-style series for the US starts in 1700, and its 1850 value was computed from census data on wages alone.
Q6120.L3f: In inflation- and PPP-adjusted 2011 prices, the 1850 US was close to subsistence, with income per person near the level of a bare-minimum survival budget of about a dollar a day.
Q6120.L4f: The correct figure is that US GDP per capita in 1850 was only about three hundred dollars in 2011 prices.

Q5849.L1t: The hearsay rules govern out-of-court statements offered to prove the truth of what they assert, and they include an exception for business records.
Q5849.L2t: The business records exception requires a foundation, usually from a custodian or other qualified witness, that the records were made at or near the time by someone with knowledge, kept in the regular course of business, and made as a regular practice.
Q5849.L3t: Records are out-of-court statements even when their maker testifies, and computer records need a showing that the process and inputs are reliable, which a bare statement that the records were kept regularly does not supply.
Q5849.L4t: The court will demand a fuller foundation showing the reliability of the computer records before admitting them.
Q5849.L2f: Computer-generated records were barred from evidence in federal courts altogether until a rules amendment in 2000 first allowed them.
Q5849.L3f: A statement falls outside the hearsay rule whenever the person who made it is present and available to testify at trial, regardless of when or where it was made.
Q5849.L4f: The hearsay objection fails because the defendant is the declarant and is available in court.
Q5849.cand_true: The court will require a greater foundation to establish the reliability of the records.
Q5849.cand_wrong1: The court will dismiss the hearsay objection because the defendant, who is the declarant, is available in court.
Q5849.cand_wrong2: The court will allow the records because they were kept in the ordinary course of business.

Q5779.L1t: A peripheral intravenous cannula is a short plastic tube placed into a vein to give fluids and drugs, and it needs regular care to stay usable.
Q5779.L2t: Flushing a cannula with saline keeps it patent and clears medication from the lumen, and it is done on a routine schedule even when the cannula is not being used.
Q5779.L3t: Guidance for cannulas that are not in continuous use sets a routine flush interval of twice daily, which is spaced at about half-day intervals.
Q5779.L4t: A cannula should be flushed every twelve hours.
Q5779.L2f: Flushing a cannula is only needed once, at insertion, because saline left in the lumen then keeps the line patent until it is removed.
Q5779.L3f: Because blood clots in an unused cannula within a few hours, standard guidance requires flushing at a short interval of about four hours, which means six flushes a day.
Q5779.L4f: A cannula should be flushed every four hours.

Q8505.L1t: Naturalism and positivism are two long-standing schools of thought in the philosophy of law and international law.
Q8505.L2t: Natural law thinking goes back to thinkers such as Grotius, while legal positivism became dominant in the nineteenth century.
Q8505.L3t: Natural law theory grounds law in objective, universal moral principles discoverable by reason, whereas positivism grounds law in what states have actually enacted or consented to.
Q8505.L4t: Naturalism rests on universal, objective rules, while positivism rests on a coherent legal order created by states according to their own interests and wishes.
Q8505.L2f: Positivism in international law was first articulated in the Middle Ages, before any notion of state sovereignty existed.
Q8505.L3f: Naturalism developed and is mainly championed by scholars outside Europe, while positivism was developed exclusively by European jurists as a regional doctrine.
Q8505.L4f: The main difference is geographic: naturalism comes from outside Europe, and positivism is a European-centred theory.
Q8505.cand_true: On the one hand, naturalism is based on a set of rules that are of universal and objective scope and on the other hand, positivism is based on a structured and coherent legal system that is created by States in light of their interests and desires
Q8505.cand_wrong1: Naturalism is a school of thought advocated outside of Europe, while positivism is Euro-centric theory
Q8505.cand_wrong2: Naturalism concerns the underpinning values of the international society, while positivism the international rules as such

Q6016.L1t: Glycolysis is the metabolic pathway that breaks glucose down into pyruvate in the cytoplasm of the cell.
Q6016.L2t: Glycolysis uses two ATP in the preparatory phase and produces four ATP in the payoff phase by substrate-level phosphorylation.
Q6016.L3t: Starting from glycogen, the first hexose is phosphorylated by phosphorylase using inorganic phosphate rather than ATP, so one fewer ATP is spent than when starting from free glucose.
Q6016.L4t: Glycolysis nets two ATP from glucose and three ATP from glycogen.
Q6016.L2f: Glycolysis takes place inside the mitochondrial matrix, where it is coupled directly to the electron transport chain.
Q6016.L3f: Glycogen entry into glycolysis costs no ATP at all and glucose entry costs one ATP, so the net yields are one apart, with glucose giving three and glycogen giving four.
Q6016.L4f: Glycolysis nets three ATP from glucose and four ATP from glycogen.

Q5584.L1t: Pew Research Center regularly surveys people in many countries about their attitudes toward democratic institutions and freedoms.
Q5584.L2t: The 2019 Pew survey asked respondents in several countries, Italy among them, how important a free media without government censorship is.
Q5584.L3t: Italy's result was a narrow majority rather than a large one, lower than in most of the other European countries surveyed.
Q5584.L4t: A little over half of Italians, a majority but not a large one, said free media is very important.
Q5584.L2f: The 2019 survey on media freedom was run by telephone among respondents in Italy only, with no other countries compared.
Q5584.L3f: Italy's figure was among the highest in Europe, above two-thirds of respondents but below four-fifths.
Q5584.L4f: Roughly seven in ten Italians said that free media without censorship is very important.

Q5999.L1t: Public opinion on school desegregation was measured by national pollsters such as Gallup across the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s.
Q5999.L2t: Support for school desegregation rose over the decades in every region, and Southern respondents were consistently less supportive than those elsewhere.
Q5999.L3t: Even at the widest point, approval in the South was well above zero and approval in the rest of the country was well short of unanimous, so the regional gap was a difference of some tens of points rather than a near-total split.
Q5999.L4t: At its peak, approval outside the South exceeded approval in the South by about forty percentage points.
Q5999.L2f: Polls on school desegregation were first taken only after the 1970s, and they found little regional variation in views.
Q5999.L3f: At the peak of the divide, almost everyone outside the South approved of school desegregation while almost no one in the South did, leaving the South nearly the full scale below the rest of the country.
Q5999.L4f: At its peak, Southern approval was about eighty percentage points below approval in the rest of the country.

Q5546.L1t: Tort law provides several theories under which a landowner can seek compensation for harm to the land from a neighbor's activities.
Q5546.L2t: Trespass to land requires a physical invasion of the land that results from the defendant's intentional act, while negligence requires breach of a duty of care that causes harm.
Q5546.L3t: The fire was accidental and not intended, and the damage came from careless upkeep of flammable residue, so liability depends on a breach of reasonable care and not on an intentional invasion.
Q5546.L4t: The neighbor would most likely recover on a negligence theory, because the mechanic failed to use reasonable care in keeping the shop free of flammable residue.
Q5546.L2f: Trespass to land has long been held to require only that the defendant's act cause something to enter the land, even if the defendant neither intended nor could foresee the entry.
Q5546.L3f: Trespass to land is satisfied by smoke drifting onto a neighbor's property from an accidental fire, since an intentional act of working with flammables suffices without any intent to intrude.
Q5546.L4f: The neighbor would most likely recover for trespass, because the smoke physically invaded the neighbor's land.

Q5113.L1t: U.S. foreign policy is shaped by the President, Congress, and a number of executive agencies.
Q5113.L2t: The National Security Council was created by the National Security Act of 1947 and is chaired by the President.
Q5113.L3t: The department headed by the Secretary of State, a Cabinet member, is the main executive department responsible for diplomacy, embassies, and carrying out foreign policy, unlike a White House advisory body or an intelligence agency.
Q5113.L4t: The State Department is the executive department that helps the President design and carry out foreign policy.
Q5113.L2f: The National Security Council was set up in the 1990s as a branch of the Pentagon and has no connection to the White House.
Q5113.L3f: The National Security Council is a full executive department with its own embassies and ambassadors, and it is the body that formally carries out U.S. foreign policy abroad.
Q5113.L4f: The National Security Council is the executive branch department that assists the President in designing and carrying out foreign policy.

Q8537.L1t: Philosophers of law debate both what punishment is and whether it can be morally justified.
Q8537.L2t: Definitions of punishment typically describe an authority deliberately inflicting unpleasant consequences on someone for an offence.
Q8537.L3t: If a moral justification were built into the definition, any argument over whether punishment is justified would be settled in advance by definition, so the definition must not presuppose any moral stance.
Q8537.L4t: Separating them matters so that the definition stays neutral on values, leaving moral justification to be argued as a separate question.
Q8537.L2f: The concept of punishment is generally agreed to have been fixed by Kant in a single, uncontested formulation.
Q8537.L3f: The reason for the separation is that punishment as an actual social institution runs independently of any moral reasons offered for it, so the two must not be run together.
Q8537.L4f: The separation matters because, in reality, the institution of punishment exists apart from any justification given for it.
Q8537.cand_true: Because any definition of punishment should be value-neutral.
Q8537.cand_wrong1: Because the practice of punishment is separate from its justification.
Q8537.cand_wrong2: Because its justification depends on the concept employed.

Q6097.L1t: Property law distinguishes between present possessory estates such as the fee simple and the fee tail, and future interests such as reversions and remainders.
Q6097.L2t: A conveyance to a person "and the heirs of his body" traditionally created a fee tail, which is an estate limited to the grantee's lineal descendants.
Q6097.L3t: Most states today treat a fee tail as a fee simple, so the wife's cousin received the entire fee simple and the grantor kept no interest to pass on.
Q6097.L4t: The niece receives nothing, because the grantor had already given away his entire interest to the cousin and had nothing left to convey to her.
Q6097.L2f: A conveyance to a person "and the heirs of his body" traditionally created a life estate that automatically ended at the grantee's death, whatever his descendants did.
Q6097.L3f: Under modern law the cousin's estate is only a life estate or fee tail, so the grantor still holds the remaining future interest and can pass it to the niece by a later deed.
Q6097.L4f: The niece holds a fee simple in the property, because the later conveyance to her was effective and gave her full ownership.
Q6097.cand_true: The conveyance gives the niece nothing because the property was already conveyed in fee simple to his wife's cousin.
Q6097.cand_wrong2: She gets a reversion in case the cousin has no heir of his body at his death.

Q8324.L1t: Dopamine is a neurotransmitter involved in reward, motivation, and movement.
Q8324.L2t: Repeated drug use causes lasting adaptations in the brain's dopamine system, and withdrawal commonly brings agitation and intense craving.
Q8324.L3t: When a drug floods the synapse with dopamine for a long time, the receiving neuron compensates by reducing how many receptors it carries, so normal dopamine levels no longer produce an effect and the person feels driven to take more.
Q8324.L4t: The patient most likely has fewer dopamine receptors on the receiving neuron, a downregulation caused by chronic drug exposure.
Q8324.L2f: Withdrawal-related agitation appears only after a single exposure to a drug and never after repeated use.
Q8324.L3f: Chronic drug use is toxic to dopamine neurons and gradually destroys them, so dopamine-rich regions lose cells and craving results.
Q8324.L4f: The patient most likely has dopamine-rich brain regions in which neurons have died.
Q8324.cand_true: There are decreased dopamine receptors on the post-synaptic membrane.
Q8324.cand_wrong1: There is cell death in the areas with high dopamine cells.
Q8324.cand_wrong2: There is seizure-like activity in the dopamine brain areas.

Q5786.L1t: Tort law limits liability to harm that is proximately caused by a defendant's negligence.
Q5786.L2t: A tortfeasor generally takes the victim as found, but an injured person's own later conduct can affect which harms are attributed to the defendant.
Q5786.L3t: The driver's negligence caused the wound and the pain before any refusal, but a refusal of treatment on religious grounds is a later independent choice that cuts off liability for the death that followed from it.
Q5786.L4t: The estate can recover for the wound and the suffering up to the moment of refusal, but not for the death itself.
Q5786.L2f: Courts have held that a person's religious objection to medical care is irrelevant to damages, because the law treats every injury as fully the original wrongdoer's responsibility.
Q5786.L3f: The pedestrian's refusal of treatment was negligent conduct that contributed to her own harm, and under contributory negligence any fault by the plaintiff bars all recovery.
Q5786.L4f: The estate should recover nothing, because the pedestrian's refusal of the transfusion was contributory negligence that bars her claim.
Q5786.cand_true: Damages for the wound and the pain and suffering up to the point that she refused the transfusion.
Q5786.cand_wrong1: No damages, because the pedestrian's refusal of treatment constitutes contributory negligence.
Q5786.cand_wrong2: All damages for wrongful death because it is foreseeable that this kind of negligence could injure someone who will not accept treatment for religious reasons.

Q5253.L1t: Property law divides ownership interests in land into present estates and future interests.
Q5253.L2t: Future interests are commonly classified by whether they are held by the transferor or by a transferee.
Q5253.L3t: When an owner conveys less than the entire estate and keeps what is left, the interest that stays with the transferor arises automatically by operation of law and needs no special words.
Q5253.L4t: The interest that stays with the original grantor after a smaller estate is carried out is the correct answer.
Q5253.L2f: Future interests in land were first recognized in the United States in the twentieth century.
Q5253.L3f: A future interest that follows a particular estate and is held by a third party who is unascertained or whose interest depends on an uncertain event is exactly what this scenario describes.
Q5253.L4f: The correct answer is the remainder in a third party that depends on an uncertain event or an unascertained person.

Q5347.L1t: Skeletal muscle contraction is powered by energy from ATP, which is regenerated through several metabolic pathways.
Q5347.L2t: Muscle cells store only a small amount of ATP, and phosphocreatine and glycolysis supply additional energy as activity continues.
Q5347.L3t: The very first energy used in a brief maximal contraction is whatever is already present in the muscle and directly usable, before any regeneration pathway has had time to start.
Q5347.L4t: The initial energy for a very high force contraction lasting 1-2 seconds comes from the ATP already stored in the muscle.
Q5347.L2f: Muscle fibers hold large ATP reserves that can power maximal contractions for about a minute before other pathways are needed.
Q5347.L3f: Even in the first second of a maximal contraction, muscle ATP is used up almost instantly, so the first energy must come from breaking down glucose through the glycolytic pathway.
Q5347.L4f: The initial energy for a very high force contraction lasting 1-2 seconds comes from glycolysis.

Q5743.L1t: Japan recovered from the devastation of World War II and became one of the world's largest economies in the postwar decades.
Q5743.L2t: Japan's economy grew very rapidly from the 1950s through the early 1970s, and then growth slowed sharply after the asset bubble burst around 1990.
Q5743.L3t: Japan's inflation-adjusted, PPP-based GDP per capita was only around $2,000 to $3,000 in 1950 and had reached roughly $38,000 to $42,000 by 2016.
Q5743.L4t: Japan's real GDP per capita rose by about fifteen times between 1950 and 2016.
Q5743.L2f: Japan's economy shrank in absolute terms during the 1960s because of strict postwar import controls, and it only began to grow again in the 1980s.
Q5743.L3f: Japan's inflation-adjusted, PPP-based GDP per capita was already about $8,000 in 1950 and was only around $40,000 in 2016, so it rose only modestly.
Q5743.L4f: Japan's real GDP per capita rose by only about five times between 1950 and 2016.

Q5028.L1t: Land subdivision law deals with how a landowner divides a tract into lots and records a plan with the county.
Q5028.L2t: The investor recorded a subdivision plan that set aside a 10-acre lot for a school, and this was publicly promoted in his brochure.
Q5028.L3t: A recorded plan that reserves a lot for a public purpose and is promoted to buyers is a dedication of that land to the public, which gives the public a right to use it and does not impose a restriction on the use of other lots.
Q5028.L4t: The designation of the 10-acre tract for a school is best described as an easement for public use.
Q5028.L2f: A subdivision plan has no legal effect on land use until the county school board formally acquires the tract by condemnation.
Q5028.L3f: The investor's designation was a promise made to the lot buyers in the plan to limit how the land is used, for the benefit of the other lots in the subdivision.
Q5028.L4f: The designation of the 10-acre tract for a school is best described as a restrictive covenant.

Q5787.L1t: Homicide offenses are graded by the defendant's mental state, ranging from intentional murder to manslaughter and offenses based on negligence.
Q5787.L2t: At common law, murder is an unlawful killing with malice aforethought, which can be shown by intent to kill, intent to cause serious bodily harm, depraved-heart recklessness, or the commission of a dangerous felony.
Q5787.L3t: The defendant deliberately fired a gun at another person, which shows recklessness with extreme disregard for human life, and the doctrine of transferred intent carries that mental state over to the unintended victim who died.
Q5787.L4t: The defendant can be convicted of murder, because firing a gun at a person shows the malice required and it transfers to the teammate who was killed.
Q5787.L2f: At common law, malice aforethought can be established only by proof that the defendant specifically intended to kill the victim.
Q5787.L3f: Because the defendant only meant to cause a slight wound and never meant to kill, the law treats his mental state as mere criminal negligence, and the death of the teammate is an accident that carries no malice.
Q5787.L4f: The defendant can be convicted only of involuntary manslaughter, because the killing of the teammate was unintended and not malicious.

Q5115.L1t: Lactate is produced in skeletal muscle when pyruvate is converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD+.
Q5115.L2t: During exercise, the rate of glycolysis and the rate of pyruvate production can exceed the rate at which mitochondria oxidise pyruvate, so some pyruvate is diverted to lactate.
Q5115.L3t: At the onset of exercise, glycolytic flux rises rapidly while oxidative metabolism takes time to catch up, so pyruvate and NADH accumulate and pyruvate is reduced to lactate.
Q5115.L4t: Muscle lactate production rises when glycolysis is switched on at the start of exercise.
Q5115.L2f: Lactate dehydrogenase converts lactate to acetyl-CoA directly inside muscle cells, which is why it is found mainly in mitochondria.
Q5115.L3f: Lactate is formed from glucose breakdown only when the pathway cannot generate pyruvate, so blocking pyruvate formation is what pushes the muscle to make lactate.
Q5115.L4f: Muscle lactate production increases when pyruvate cannot be formed from glucose breakdown.
Q5115.cand_true: glycolysis is activated at the onset of exercise.
Q5115.cand_wrong1: pyruvate cannot be formed from glucose breakdown.

Q6111.L1t: The First Amendment limits government restrictions on speech, and it applies to state and city governments through the Fourteenth Amendment.
Q6111.L2t: The Supreme Court has recognized that some expressive conduct, such as wearing armbands or burning a flag, can count as symbolic speech.
Q6111.L3t: A littering ban applies to everyone whatever message they intend, and the city's interest in clean parks has nothing to do with the protestor's message, so any burden on expression is incidental and the ordinance passes intermediate scrutiny.
Q6111.L4t: The protestor may be prosecuted, because the ordinance is content-neutral, serves a substantial government interest, and is not aimed at suppressing expression.
Q6111.L2f: The Supreme Court first recognized the idea of symbolic speech in a case about a tax on newspaper advertising revenue.
Q6111.L3f: The First Amendment protects only spoken or written words, so a physical act like dumping trash falls outside its scope however much the actor means to communicate by it.
Q6111.L4f: The protestor may be prosecuted, because dumping trash is an act rather than expression and so cannot be treated as communication.
Q6111.cand_true: Yes, because the city ordinance advances an important and legitimate public interest and is not directed at the suppression of communication.
Q6111.cand_wrong1: Yes, because littering the park is conduct, not speech and, therefore, it may not be treated by the law as communication.
Q6111.cand_wrong2: No, because littering the park in these circumstances could be construed as symbolic speech and, thus, it is protected from government regulation by the First and Fourteenth Amendments.

Q5735.L1t: Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction, and removal allows certain actions filed in state court to be moved to federal court.
Q5735.L2t: Removal is governed by 28 U.S.C. 1441, and a motion to remand based on a procedural defect in removal must be made within thirty days of the notice of removal.
Q5735.L3t: The removal statute gives the power to remove only to defendants, so a plaintiff who chose to sue in state court cannot remove her own case, even when it includes federal claims.
Q5735.L4t: The federal court will send the entire case back to state court because the plaintiff had no right to remove it.
Q5735.L2f: Removal of a federal-question case is allowed only if the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000.
Q5735.L3f: Any party to a state-court action, plaintiff or defendant, may remove it once a federal claim appears in the complaint, provided notice is filed within thirty days.
Q5735.L4f: The court will keep the case, because the removal was timely and the complaint includes federal claims.
Q5735.cand_wrong1: Retain the case, because it was timely removed and the woman alleges federal claims.
Q5735.cand_wrong2: Retain the case to avoid the risk of bias and impropriety in having it proceed before a judge who has shown clear hostility toward the woman's attorney.

Q5541.L1t: The Pew Research Center surveys attitudes toward religion and morality in many countries, including India.
Q5541.L2t: Pew's 2019 survey on belief in God and morality covered 34 countries, and India was among the countries where tying morality to belief in God was far more common than in Western Europe.
Q5541.L3t: Pew's 2019 figure for India was above three-quarters of respondents but well short of nine in ten.
Q5541.L4t: The share of Indians who say belief in God is necessary for morality is just under eighty percent, in the high seventies.
Q5541.L2f: Pew first asked this question in India in 2005 and surveyed only Hindu respondents.
Q5541.L3f: Pew found that only a modest majority of Indians, a little under six in ten, link morality to belief in God, well below most other surveyed developing countries.
Q5541.L4f: The share of Indians who say belief in God is necessary for morality is in the high fifties, about six in ten.

Q5365.L1t: Pet food brands in the United States use memorable advertising slogans and jingles to market their products to cat owners.
Q5365.L2t: The slogan about cats asking for a food by name is part of a long-running advertising campaign that features a catchy jingle.
Q5365.L3t: The brand whose jingle is sung by cats repeating its own two-word name, with the line that cats 'ask for it by name,' is the one built on a meowing-sound name.
Q5365.L4t: The brand that claims cats ask for it by name is the one whose name is a pair of words imitating a cat's meow.
Q5365.L2f: The 'ask for it by name' slogan was first introduced in the 1920s as part of a radio campaign for a canned fish product.
Q5365.L3f: The 'cats ask for it by name' claim belongs to the premium gourmet line that is marketed with elegant, upscale imagery and the word 'Feast' in its title.

Q5651.L1t: Sales of goods such as automobiles are governed by Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code.
Q5651.L2t: Under the UCC, a seller's description of the goods, including in an advertisement, can become part of the basis of the bargain and create an express warranty.
Q5651.L3t: A disclaimer clause is inoperative to the extent it conflicts with an express warranty, and a clause saying goods are sold in their current condition excludes implied warranties but cannot undo the seller's specific promise about what the car is, here its model year.
Q5651.L4t: Carol should win, because the clause saying the car is sold in its current condition cannot cancel the seller's express promise that the car was a 1964 model.
Q5651.L2f: The UCC requires that every contract for the sale of a used car be notarized before it is enforceable.
Q5651.L3f: A seller is liable for misdescribing goods only if the buyer proves the seller was careless, because express warranty liability depends on fault.
Q5651.L4f: The seller wins unless Carol can show carelessness in how the picture was presented, so the contract language protects the seller otherwise.
Q5651.cand_true: Carol, because the "as is" disclosure was not totally effective.
Q5651.cand_wrong1: The seller, unless they were negligent in not explicitly stating the picture was of a new car, not the actual car to be sold.
Q5651.cand_wrong2: Carol, because the internet picture was of a car that had never been driven, not the actual used car she was to buy.

Q5004.L1t: Future interests such as executory interests follow a defeasible estate and can cut it short when a stated event occurs.
Q5004.L2t: The Rule Against Perpetuities voids a contingent interest unless it must vest or fail within a life in being at creation plus twenty-one years.
Q5004.L3t: The gift is to a class of the sister's children who reach 25, and the class can include children born long after the grant, and the church-use condition could be triggered at any remote time, so nothing guarantees the interest vests or fails within lives in being plus 21 years.
Q5004.L4t: The executory interest in the sister's children is void under the Rule Against Perpetuities, which leaves the friend holding the entire title.
Q5004.L2f: A general warranty deed covers only title defects that arose during the grantor's own period of ownership.
Q5004.L3f: The sister is a life in being, so every child she bears in her lifetime is counted, and the interest must vest or fail within her lifetime, which satisfies the Rule Against Perpetuities.
Q5004.L4f: The gift over to the sister's children is valid, so title is shared by the friend and every child the sister bears during her lifetime, whether or not already born.
Q5004.cand_wrong1: the friend, the son, the daughter, and any additional children of the sister born during her lifetime.
Q5004.cand_wrong2: the friend, the son, the daughter, and any additional children of the sister born within 21 years after the death of the deceased son.

Q5133.L1t: M&M's are candy-coated chocolates made by Mars, Incorporated and sold in many varieties.
Q5133.L2t: M&M's advertising features animated candy characters that talk, argue and star in commercials as the brand's spokescandies.
Q5133.L3t: The two lead spokescandies are named for the color of their candy shells, and they represent the plain and peanut varieties.
Q5133.L4t: The two primary spokescandies are named after their shell colors, red and yellow.

Q8166.L1t: Henry Maine was a 19th-century legal historian whose book Ancient Law examined how early legal systems developed.

Q9014.L3t: Under the prevailing modern approach, the agency theory, felony murder liability attaches only when the killing is done by a felon or someone acting in concert with the felons, and a police officer is neither.
Q9014.L4t: The appellate court will likely reverse, because most jurisdictions do not apply felony murder when a third party kills a co-felon.
Q9014.L2f: Felony murder was abolished in most states after courts found that it conflicted with constitutional due process requirements.
Q9014.L3f: Under the prevailing modern approach, the proximate cause theory is universally adopted, so every death that results from the felony is attributed to the felons regardless of who fires the fatal shot.
Q9014.L4f: The appellate court will likely affirm, because every state holds felony murder applies to any death during the crime no matter who fired the fatal shot.
Q9014.cand_true: Yes, because the majority view is that felony murder does not apply if a co-conspirator is killed by a third person during the commission of the crime.
Q9014.cand_wrong1: No, because all states recognize that felony murder applies to any deaths that occur during the commission of the crime regardless of who fired the fatal shot.
Q9014.cand_wrong2: No, because the man started the flurry of shots instead of surrendering; he caused the woman's death and is guilty of first degree murder.

Q9015.L1t: Cells carry out metabolism through networks of chemical reactions that are mostly catalyzed by enzymes.
Q9015.L2t: Enzymes, which catalyze nearly all metabolic reactions, are proteins.
Q9015.L3t: Genes encode the sequences of proteins, so the cell's enzymes, and therefore which reactions it can perform, are set by its genetic material.
Q9015.L4t: Metabolism is determined by the proteins that are made according to the instructions in the genetic material.
Q9015.L2f: Metabolic reactions in cells proceed without enzymes at the same rates, so proteins play little role in them.
Q9015.L3f: The supply of free amino acids in the cell is the limiting factor that sets which metabolic reactions occur and how fast, regardless of which genes are present.
Q9015.L4f: Metabolism is determined by how many amino acids are available to the cell.
Q9015.cand_true: proteins formed as dictated by the genetic material.
Q9015.cand_wrong2: amino acid composition of the ribonucleic acids.

Q9016.L1t: The United States has urbanized steadily since the nineteenth century, with most people now living in cities and suburbs.
Q9016.L2t: The Census Bureau defines urban areas by population size and density, and counts both large cities and smaller urbanized clusters.
Q9016.L3t: Census figures show that a little over four-fifths of the U.S. population lived in urban areas in the 2010s, and the share was still below nine-tenths.
Q9016.L4t: In 2017, about four in five Americans, a little over 80 percent, lived in urban areas.
Q9016.L2f: The Census Bureau counts only people living inside the limits of incorporated cities as urban, which leaves out suburban residents.
Q9016.L3f: Census estimates show that nearly all Americans, more than nine in ten, lived in urban areas by the late 2010s.
Q9016.L4f: In 2017, about 92 percent of Americans lived in urban areas.

Q9017.L1t: A joint tenancy with right of survivorship gives co-owners equal undivided interests, and on one owner's death the survivor takes the whole property.
Q9017.L2t: A joint tenancy can be severed by a transfer of one owner's interest, after which the co-owners hold as tenants in common with no survivorship.
Q9017.L3t: In a lien theory state a mortgage only creates a security interest and does not transfer title, so it does not sever the joint tenancy, and the lien ends when the borrowing owner dies and the survivor's interest takes over.
Q9017.L4t: The bank cannot enforce the mortgage, because the lien did not sever the joint tenancy and the surviving partner owns the property outright.
Q9017.L2f: In a lien theory state, a mortgage gives the lender legal title to the property until the debt is paid off.
Q9017.L3f: Under the majority view, any mortgage by one joint tenant transfers title to the lender and so severs the joint tenancy, leaving the lender holding a lien that survives the borrower's death.
Q9017.L4f: The bank can enforce the mortgage, because it severed the joint tenancy and gave the bank title and a lien it can foreclose after the partner's death.
Q9017.cand_true: No, the mortgage lien could not destroy the joint tenancy, and when the partner dies, the property passes by operation of law to the surviving joint tenant.
Q9017.cand_wrong1: Yes, the bank got title to the property by virtue of the mortgage, which destroyed the joint tenancy, and it can execute on its lien.
Q9017.cand_wrong2: No, although the mortgage destroyed the joint tenancy, the bank has to get a deed of trust in order to execute on jointly owned property.

Q9018.L1t: Contract law generally requires a bargained-for exchange of legal value before a promise is enforceable.
Q9018.L2t: Covenants not to compete are enforced only if they are reasonable in duration, geography and scope, and are supported by consideration.
Q9018.L3t: When an employer who could have discharged an at-will employee instead keeps her on for years after she signs, that forbearance counts as value given in exchange for her promise.
Q9018.L4t: The employer can enforce the covenant, because years of continued employment after signing supplied valid consideration.
Q9018.L2f: Covenants not to compete are governed by the Uniform Commercial Code rather than by common-law contract rules.
Q9018.L3f: Under the governing rule, a covenant signed after hiring is just a change to the existing employment deal, and such changes bind the parties even if one side gives nothing new.
Q9018.L4f: The employer can enforce the covenant because it merely altered an existing contract, and that needs no new consideration.
Q9018.cand_true: Yes, because the employer's providing of continued employment for a substantial period after signing the covenant is adequate consideration.
Q9018.cand_wrong1: Yes, because modification of an existing contract does not require consideration.
Q9018.cand_wrong2: No, because there was inadequate consideration for the covenant.

Q9019.L1t: Repeated sprint sports depend on rapid ATP regeneration from phosphocreatine and anaerobic glycolysis.
Q9019.L2t: During intense exercise, muscle converts ADP to AMP through adenylate kinase, and AMP is then deaminated to IMP.
Q9019.L3t: Deamination of AMP to IMP releases ammonia, and IMP is then degraded along the purine pathway, whose intermediate and end product in humans are hypoxanthine and uric acid.
Q9019.L4t: Blood ammonia, hypoxanthine and uric acid all rise as products of adenine nucleotide breakdown during repeated sprints.
Q9019.L2f: In sprint sports, ADP degradation takes place almost entirely in the liver rather than in the working muscle.
Q9019.L3f: Adenine nucleotide breakdown in working muscle is cleared mainly through the urea cycle and through the creatine waste pathway, not through purine intermediates.
Q9019.L4f: The ADP degradation products that rise in the blood during repeated sprints are ammonia, urea and creatinine.

Q9020.L1t: A will governs property passing at death, while a deed transfers interests during the grantor's life.
Q9020.L2t: Florida lets a prospective spouse waive rights such as the elective share and the pretermitted spouse share through a valid prenuptial agreement.
Q9020.L3t: A deed delivered during life to himself and his spouse as tenants by the entirety gives her a survivorship right that takes the property outside the will, and her valid waiver bars any claim against the rest of the estate.
Q9020.L4t: Kathy takes the condominium by survivorship, and the prenuptial waiver bars any further share, so Tommy gets the pasture land and the children split the residue.
Q9020.L2f: Florida requires a prenuptial agreement to be recorded with the county clerk before it has any effect on probate.
Q9020.L3f: A prenuptial waiver cannot defeat the share of a spouse married after the will was signed, because that statutory share applies automatically.
Q9020.L4f: Kathy is a pretermitted spouse despite the prenuptial agreement, so she takes half of the estate.
Q9020.cand_true: Kathy gets the condominium regardless of the prenuptial agreement, Tommy takes the pasture land and Tommy and Julie split the rest of the estate.
Q9020.cand_wrong1: Regardless of the prenuptial agreement, Kathy is a pretermitted spouse. Since Bill leaves surviving lineal descendants who are not Kathy's, Kathy receives 50% of the estate, Tommy gets the pasture land, and Tommy and Julie split the residue of the estate.
Q9020.cand_wrong2: Due to Kathy's prenuptial agreement, Tommy receives the pasture land, Julie gets the condominium and Tommy and Julie split the rest of the estate.

Q9021.L1t: Property law separates real property from personal property, and the line is often drawn by how an item is attached to land or a building.
Q9021.L2t: Courts usually decide whether an item is a fixture by looking at how it is annexed to the property, how well it is adapted to it, and what the person who attached it intended.
Q9021.L3t: Items custom-made for a house and firmly screwed and bracketed to its window frames are ordinarily treated as part of the realty, so they pass to the purchaser unless the contract says otherwise, and the seller's later removal does not change that.
Q9021.L4t: The buyer is likely to win because the custom shutters were attached to the house in a way that made them fixtures, so they passed with the home.
Q9021.L2f: The law of fixtures was created mainly by federal statute in the twentieth century and has no roots in the common law.
Q9021.L3f: Once a seller removes an attached item and restores the property to its original condition, the item is treated as personal property again and the buyer loses any claim to it.
Q9021.L4f: The buyer is unlikely to prevail, because the seller's repair and repainting of the window frames after taking the shutters off defeats the claim.
Q9021.cand_true: Yes, because the shutters had become fixtures.
Q9021.cand_wrong1: No, because the window frames had been repaired and repainted after removal of the shutters.
Q9021.cand_wrong2: No, because the sales agreement did not mention the shutters.

Q9022.L1t: Transparency International runs surveys that measure how ordinary citizens experience corruption in different regions of the world.
Q9022.L2t: Mexico was one of the Latin American countries covered by the 2017 Global Corruption Barometer, which asked service users whether they had paid a bribe in the previous twelve months.
Q9022.L3t: Mexico's rate was far above the Latin American regional average of roughly 29%, yet bribery was not reported by nearly all service users.
Q9022.L4t: About half of Mexican respondents, a little over fifty percent, reported paying a bribe for public services.
Q9022.L2f: The 2017 barometer was carried out only as a telephone poll of Mexican government officials, not of ordinary citizens.
Q9022.L3f: Mexico's bribery rate in 2017 was close to the Latin American regional average of roughly 30%, with fewer than one in three service users reporting a bribe.
Q9022.L4f: Only about three in ten Mexican respondents reported paying a bribe for public services.

Q9023.L1t: Many American and British cities have traditional nicknames for their residents that come from local history.
Q9023.L2t: The word Knickerbocker comes from a Dutch-sounding surname that Washington Irving made famous through a satirical work of fiction.
Q9023.L3t: Washington Irving's 1809 satirical history, written under the pseudonym Diedrich Knickerbocker, poked fun at the Dutch colonial settlement of New Amsterdam, and the name became linked to that settlement's descendants and its later city.
Q9023.L4t: The residents known as Knickerbockers are the people of New York City.
Q9023.L2f: The word Knickerbocker was invented in the 1920s by a newspaper advertising campaign and had no earlier use.
Q9023.L3f: The name Knickerbocker began with the Thames watermen and traders of seventeenth-century England, who were called by that name.
Q9023.L4f: Knickerbockers is the traditional name for the people of London.

Q9024.L1t: Criminal law recognizes defenses such as self-defense, and an arrest's legality can matter to an assault charge.
Q9024.L2t: At common law a person may resist an unlawful arrest with reasonable force, but statutes like this one restrict that right when the person knows an officer is arresting them.
Q9024.L3t: Such a statute covers resisting a proper arrest and does not take away the right to defend against excessive force, so if the officer began beating the suspect without provocation, the suspect's blow was privileged self-defense whether or not the arrest was lawful.
Q9024.L4t: If the jury accepts the suspect's version, he acted in self-defense against excessive force and must be acquitted, provided the arrest itself was lawful.
Q9024.L2f: The statute applies only to arrests made with a warrant, and it also bars any later claim of self-defense.
Q9024.L3f: Once an arrest is unlawful, the person arrested loses all privilege to use force, so any blow he strikes at the officer is a crime whichever version of events is true.
Q9024.L4f: The suspect should be found guilty whenever the arrest was unlawful, no matter which account the jury believes.
Q9024.cand_true: not guilty, if the arrest was lawful, provided that the jury believes the suspect's account.
Q9024.cand_wrong1: guilty, if the arrest was unlawful, regardless which account the jury believes.
Q9024.cand_wrong2: not guilty, if the arrest was unlawful without probable cause and the jury believes the suspect's account.

Q9025.L1t: Property law governs the conflicting rights of neighboring landowners to use and enjoy their land.
Q9025.L2t: Traditional English-derived law gave landowners no natural right to light and air, but some modern courts have reconsidered that rule for solar-heated homes.
Q9025.L3t: Compliance with zoning and building rules does not shield a use from nuisance liability, and a use that substantially and unreasonably interferes with a neighbor's enjoyment of her land can be enjoined, especially where a harmless alternative placement exists.
Q9025.L4t: The appellate court will likely reverse, because the planned house would be a private nuisance that unreasonably interferes with the owner's use and enjoyment of her property.
Q9025.L2f: Under the traditional rule, every landowner automatically holds a perpetual easement to receive sunlight across neighboring land.
Q9025.L3f: Courts weigh the social utility of the defendant's use against the harm to the plaintiff, and a lawful use that follows zoning and building law is presumed to outweigh a neighbor's private interest in sunlight, even when a less harmful placement exists.
Q9025.L4f: The appellate court will likely affirm, because weighing the benefits and burdens on each side favors the neighbor who wants to build.
Q9025.cand_true: Yes, because the proposed use is a private nuisance that unreasonably interferes with the owner's use and enjoyment of her property.
Q9025.cand_wrong1: No, because a comparative evaluation of the benefits and detriments of each position favor the neighbor's position.
Q9025.cand_wrong2: Yes, because blocking a neighbor's sunlight is a constitutional deprivation of substantive due process.

Q9026.L1t: Jumper cables are used to start a car with a dead battery by borrowing power from another vehicle's battery.
Q9026.L2t: Jumper cables come in pairs of clamps, with one color conventionally marking the positive connection and a different color marking the negative.
Q9026.L3t: The red clamp marks the positive terminal, and by convention the other cable in the pair is black, which marks the negative connection.
Q9026.L4t: The negative connector on a set of jumper cables is colored black.
Q9026.L2f: Jumper cable colors are set by a federal law that assigns a different color to each of the four clamps.
Q9026.L3f: Orange is the safety color reserved for ground and negative connections on automotive cables, while the remaining colors are used for positive leads.
Q9026.L4f: The negative connector on a set of jumper cables is colored orange.

Q9027.L1t: Law is commonly divided into branches such as criminal law, civil law, and commercial law, each governing different kinds of disputes.
Q9027.L2t: Stare decisis is the principle that courts follow precedent set by earlier decisions, and it operates within the common-law system.
Q9027.L3t: A body of law that defines the rights between private persons and gives a remedy, such as damages, when those rights are violated is the branch that handles private disputes, not offenses against the state or rules of precedent.
Q9027.L4t: The answer is civil law, the branch that establishes rights between persons and provides redress when they are violated.
Q9027.L2f: Stare decisis is a Latin phrase that originated in ancient Roman statutes and is codified in the federal constitution as a list of private rights.
Q9027.L3f: Stare decisis is the body of law that creates rights between individuals and supplies remedies when those rights are violated, since precedent itself defines private entitlements and redress.
Q9027.L4f: The answer is stare decisis, which is the body of law establishing rights between persons and providing redress for their violation.

Q9028.L1t: Surveys by organizations such as Pew and Gallup regularly measure American attitudes toward press freedom and the news media.
Q9028.L2t: The First Amendment protects freedom of the press in the United States, and public opinion polls have long tracked how much Americans value it.
Q9028.L3t: The 2019 survey found that the great majority of Americans, roughly four in five, rated an uncensored free media as very important, which is a higher share than seven in ten.
Q9028.L4t: About eighty percent of Americans said in 2019 that it is very important to have free media without government censorship.
Q9028.L2f: Polls on press freedom in the United States have only been conducted since 2015, and they were limited to adults under thirty.
Q9028.L3f: The 2019 survey found that about seven in ten Americans rated free media without state censorship as very important, with the remaining three in ten saying it was not very important.
Q9028.L4f: About seventy percent of Americans said in 2019 that it is very important to have free media without government censorship.

Q9029.L1t: Bladder washout is a nursing procedure in which fluid is flushed through a urinary catheter to clear blockages or debris.
Q9029.L2t: Sterile 0.9% sodium chloride is the standard solution recommended for bladder washout, and the procedure is typically done with an aseptic technique through a catheter.
Q9029.L3t: Water is hypotonic compared with body fluids, so when it contacts the bladder lining it can be absorbed into the circulation and disturb the balance of sodium and other electrolytes.
Q9029.L4t: The risk is that using water can upset the body's electrolyte balance.
Q9029.L2f: Bladder washout in secondary care is performed only once per patient, and the solution is always warmed to above 50 degrees Celsius before use.
Q9029.L3f: Water is thicker than saline and clings to the catheter and bladder wall, so it tends to leak around the catheter rather than drain, and its main risk is that fluid escapes past the catheter.
Q9029.L4f: The risk of using water is that fluid may bypass the catheter when the washout is carried out.
Q9029.cand_true: Using water may cause electrolyte imbalance.
Q9029.cand_wrong1: Fluid may bypass when the washout is carried out.

Q9030.L1t: Third-party beneficiary law is the part of contract law that decides when someone who is not a party to a contract can enforce it.
Q9030.L2t: A person who is not a party can enforce a contract only if the parties intended to benefit them, and that intent is judged from the terms and circumstances of the agreement.
Q9030.L3t: A beneficiary's rights do not vest until they learn of the promise and accept it or rely on it, so until then the original parties can modify or discharge the arrangement by mutual agreement.
Q9030.L4t: Because the son knew nothing and had not relied when the owner and landscaper agreed to redirect payment, that modification was effective and the son cannot recover from the owner.
Q9030.L2f: The third-party beneficiary doctrine was first recognized in American law by the Uniform Commercial Code, and it had no common-law origin.
Q9030.L3f: A named beneficiary's rights vest the moment the contract is signed, so the original parties can never change the payee afterward without that beneficiary's consent.
Q9030.L4f: The son was an intended beneficiary whose right to the money could be enforced against the owner, so he will win his suit.
Q9030.cand_true: not prevail, because the owner and the landscaper effectively modified their agreement, thereby depriving the son of any rights he may have had.
Q9030.cand_wrong1: prevail, because the son was the intended beneficiary under the terms of the written contract between the owner and the landscaper.
Q9030.cand_wrong2: prevail, because the written contract between the owner and the landscaper operated as a valid assignment to the son.

Q9031.L1t: Assignment of contract rights is governed by a mix of common-law principles and Uniform Commercial Code provisions for the sale of goods.
Q9031.L2t: Contract rights are generally freely assignable unless the assignment would materially change the other party's duty, increase their burden or risk, or reduce their chance of getting return performance.
Q9031.L3t: Under the UCC and the common-law approach to interpretation, a general clause barring assignment is read to prevent delegation of performance, not transfer of the right to payment, unless the clause specifically says otherwise.
Q9031.L4t: The court will not apply the general anti-assignment clause to block the transfer of the right to payment, because the clause does not specifically cover it.
Q9031.L2f: At common law, contract rights could never be assigned under any circumstances, and only modern statutes made assignment possible.
Q9031.L3f: Courts presume that a general no-assignment clause also reaches payment rights, because protecting the obligor from having to pay a stranger is strongly preferred.
Q9031.L4f: The court will enforce the general bar and block the distributor's assignment of its right to the funds.
Q9031.cand_true: No, a bar of assignment does not apply to the right to receive the funds unless specifically stated.
Q9031.cand_wrong1: Yes, a bar against the right to receive proceeds is a favored restriction unless otherwise stated.
Q9031.cand_wrong2: Yes, a contractual provision prohibiting assignments is enforceable in all respects.

Q9032.L1t: India is the second most populous country in the world, with more than 1.3 billion people in 2017.
Q9032.L2t: India's urban population share has risen steadily since independence, from roughly 17 percent in 1951.
Q9032.L3t: In 2017 agriculture and village life still sheltered a clear majority of Indians, with roughly two-thirds of the population living in rural areas.
Q9032.L4t: About one in three Indians lived in cities and towns in 2017.
Q9032.L2f: India's national Census has been conducted every five years since 1951.
Q9032.L3f: By 2017 India's rural population had shrunk to little more than a third of the total, and most people lived in cities.
Q9032.L4f: In 2017 nearly two-thirds of Indians lived in urban areas.

Q9033.L1t: Treaty interpretation in international law is largely governed by the rules codified in the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.
Q9033.L2t: The general rule of interpretation appears in Article 31 of the Vienna Convention, while Article 32 separately addresses supplementary means such as preparatory work.
Q9033.L3t: Article 31 sets out a single combined rule in which good faith, the ordinary meaning of terms, their context, and the treaty's object and purpose are all weighed together, rather than any one element standing alone.
Q9033.L4t: Treaties are to be interpreted in good faith, giving the terms their ordinary meaning in their context and in light of the treaty's object and purpose.
Q9033.L2f: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties was adopted in 1969 and sets its interpretation rules in Article 5, which applies only to bilateral treaties.
Q9033.L3f: Under the Vienna Convention's interpretive rule, the treaty's object and purpose is the sole controlling criterion, and the wording of the text and its context carry no independent weight.
Q9033.L4f: Treaties are to be interpreted solely in light of their object and purpose, with no separate regard to the ordinary meaning of the terms.
Q9033.cand_true: Treaties are to be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given to the terms of the treaty in their context and in the light of its object and purpose
Q9033.cand_wrong1: Treaties are to be interpreted only in light of its object and purpose
Q9033.cand_wrong2: Treaties are to be interpreted in accordance with the intention of the parties, as evidenced in the preparatory works of the treaty

Q9034.L1t: Military spending is usually measured both in absolute dollars and as a share of a country's gross domestic product.
Q9034.L2t: The United States has the largest military budget in the world in absolute terms, though its share of GDP is well below its Cold War levels.
Q9034.L3t: US defense outlays in 2017 were roughly 600 to 700 billion dollars against a GDP of about 19 trillion dollars, which works out to a low single-digit percentage.
Q9034.L4t: In 2017 the United States spent about three percent of its GDP on the military.
Q9034.L2f: US military spending as a share of GDP has been rising steadily since the end of the Cold War and reached its postwar peak in 2017.
Q9034.L3f: In 2017 US defense spending was roughly 1.9 trillion dollars, around a tenth of the country's roughly 19 trillion dollar GDP.
Q9034.L4f: In 2017 the United States spent about ten percent of its GDP on the military.

Q9035.L1t: Ross Perot ran as an independent candidate in the 1992 US presidential election against George H. W. Bush and Bill Clinton.
Q9035.L2t: Perot withdrew from the race in July 1992, then re-entered in October and took part in the televised presidential debates.
Q9035.L3t: Perot's final share was the strongest for a non-major-party candidate since Theodore Roosevelt in 1912, and it was close to one fifth of all votes cast.
Q9035.L4t: Perot finished with about nineteen percent of the popular vote.
Q9035.L2f: Perot won several states outright in 1992 and carried electoral votes in the Mountain West.
Q9035.L3f: Perot's support collapsed after his mid-race withdrawal, and his final share was well under ten percent, similar to a typical minor-party candidate.
Q9035.L4f: Perot finished with about seven percent of the popular vote.

Q9036.L1t: Scars form as part of the normal healing process after skin is injured, and their appearance varies between individuals.
Q9036.L2t: Keloids tend to be more common in people with darker skin and often develop after surgery, burns or other skin injury.
Q9036.L3t: A keloid results from excessive collagen deposition that grows beyond the original wound edges, producing a raised, thick, dense area of tissue.
Q9036.L4t: A keloid is a firm, raised mass of scar tissue.
Q9036.L2f: Keloids occur almost exclusively in very young infants and never develop after surgical incisions.
Q9036.L3f: A keloid forms when too little collagen is laid down, so the healed wound remains flat, narrow and barely visible.
Q9036.L4f: A keloid is a fine, hairline scar.
Q9036.cand_true: a firm mass of scar tissue.
Q9036.cand_wrong2: formed if a wound drain is removed too soon.

Q9037.L1t: A tracheostomy is a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the neck into the windpipe, and it can be temporary or permanent.
Q9037.L2t: A tracheostomy bypasses the upper airway, and the tube placed in the opening may be cuffed or uncuffed depending on the patient's needs.
Q9037.L3t: A tracheostomy tube lets sedation be reduced and gives direct access to the airway, so ventilator support can be lowered in steps as breathing recovers.
Q9037.L4t: A tracheostomy can be used to help wean patients off a ventilator.
Q9037.L2f: A tracheostomy tube is always placed above the vocal cords, and it is inserted through the mouth rather than through the neck.
Q9037.L3f: A tracheostomy tube sits at the level of the larynx and acts as a support that restores vocal cord movement, so it directly treats the paralysed cords.
Q9037.L4f: A tracheostomy is done to repair the vocal cords after paralysis.
Q9037.cand_true: As an aid to weaning patients from a ventilator.
Q9037.cand_wrong1: To repair vocal cords after paralysis.

Q9038.L1t: Osteopathic manipulative treatment includes many techniques, such as articulatory, muscle energy and soft tissue methods, each with its own risks and contraindications.
Q9038.L2t: The vertebral arteries pass through the cervical transverse foramina and can be vulnerable to vertebrobasilar insufficiency, especially in older patients.
Q9038.L3t: Combined rotation and extension of the neck stretches and narrows the vertebral arteries, which can reduce blood flow to the brainstem and cause confusion, nausea and vertigo.
Q9038.L4t: The physician may be liable if the neck was treated in simultaneous hyperrotation and extension.
Q9038.L2f: Cervical manipulation affects only the paraspinal muscles, and the arteries of the neck are not mechanically affected by neck positioning.
Q9038.L3f: Osteoarthritis of the cervical spine is an absolute contraindication to any neck treatment, so treating such a patient at all is a clear breach of the standard of care.
Q9038.L4f: The physician may be liable if the patient was previously treated for osteoarthritis of the cervical spine.
Q9038.cand_true: the neck was treated in simultaneous hyperrotation and extension
Q9038.cand_wrong1: the patient was previously treated for osteoarthritis of the cervical spine
Q9038.cand_wrong2: the motion barrier was articulated more than 3 times

Q9039.L1t: Murder generally requires a killing committed with malice, which includes intent to kill, intent to inflict serious bodily harm, or a depraved-heart disregard for human life.
Q9039.L2t: Under the common law, a bare failure to act does not create criminal liability unless the defendant owed a legal duty to the victim, such as one arising from a special relationship like marriage.
Q9039.L3t: A spouse owes a legal duty to rescue or warn the other spouse, and a person who knowingly and deliberately breaches that duty out of hatred, aware that death is imminent, acts with the malice required for murder.
Q9039.L4t: The defendant who watches her husband walk toward a hidden gunman and deliberately withholds a warning because she hates him is the one most likely guilty of murder.
Q9039.L2f: Under the common law, an omission to act can never support any criminal conviction, and legal duties arising from relationships such as marriage have no effect on liability.
Q9039.L3f: Lending a car to a person known to be severely intoxicated shows extreme recklessness and a conscious disregard for human life, and the lender's act of providing the car is the direct cause of any resulting death.
Q9039.L4f: The defendant who knowingly lets an obviously intoxicated friend drive his car is the one most likely guilty of murder, since lending the car to her shows depraved-heart malice.
Q9039.cand_true: The defendant hates her husband after learning that he is having an affair with her best friend. She also knows that her husband owes a man a large amount of money, which he refuses to pay. Before the husband is about to leave for work, the defendant looks out the window and sees the man hiding outside with a gun. The defendant decides not to warn the husband, who then walks outside and is shot and killed by the man.
Q9039.cand_wrong1: The defendant and his friend attended a party together. At the party, the friend became extremely inebriated. The friend asked the defendant if she could borrow his car to drive to the liquor store to buy more booze for the party. Although the defendant was aware of the friend's intoxicated condition, he allowed her to drive his car to the liquor store. The friend drove through a red light and collided with the victim's car.
